common_name: Centennial Spirit Crape Myrtle (Dark Foliage Deep Red Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Centennial Spirit is a Carl Whitcomb introduction grown for the contrast between its dusky bronze-purple new foliage and deep wine-red flower clusters.

directions: Centennial Spirit is a Carl Whitcomb introduction valued for deep wine-red flower clusters set against dusky bronze-purple new foliage that settles into a more subdued bronze-green through summer heat. It grows into a well-branched, upright small tree reaching 15 to 20 feet, developing mottled gray-and-tan exfoliating bark with age. Bloom is heaviest in early-to-mid summer with a lighter rebloom flush if spent panicles are removed, and it shows good resistance to powdery mildew for a Lagerstroemia indica selection, though full sun and open air circulation still help keep foliage clean. Avoid topping the tree; remove only dead, crossing, or sucker growth each winter to preserve its natural vase shape.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Crape Myrtle Cultivars

common_name: Ebony Fire Crape Myrtle (Near-Black Foliage Cherry-Red Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs or small trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Ebony Fire is part of the Whitcomb-bred Ebony series grown for near-black foliage paired with vivid red flowers.

directions: Ebony Fire is part of the Whitcomb-bred Ebony series, prized for foliage that emerges near-black and holds its deep purple-maroon cast through the growing season, setting off clusters of vivid cherry-red flowers from early summer into fall. Plants form a dense, well-branched small tree or large shrub to roughly 10 to 12 feet, with smooth gray-tan bark that exfoliates modestly compared to the boldest National Arboretum hybrids. It shows good resistance to powdery mildew for an indica-type selection, though full sun and open air circulation still help in humid Gulf South summers. Deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage a second flush of bloom, and prune only to remove dead or crossing wood in late winter rather than topping the plant.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Crape Myrtle Cultivars

common_name: Ebony Flame Crape Myrtle (Near-Black Foliage Orange-Red Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs or small trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Ebony Flame is part of the Whitcomb-bred Ebony series, combining near-black foliage with bright orange-red flowers.

directions: Ebony Flame shares the Ebony series' near-black spring foliage, which matures to a deep bronze-purple through summer, but sets it off with brighter orange-red flower clusters rather than the straight red of its Ebony Fire sibling. It matures into a rounded, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree to roughly 10 to 12 feet, with a dense branching habit well suited to a specimen planting where the dark foliage reads clearly against a lighter background. Powdery mildew resistance is good for an indica-type selection, though full sun and good air circulation still help keep foliage clean in humid summers. Deadhead after the first flush for repeat bloom, and limit pruning to removing dead, crossing, or sucker growth in late winter.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Crape Myrtle Cultivars

common_name: Ebony Glow Crape Myrtle (Near-Black Foliage White-Flowered Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs or small trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Ebony Glow is part of the Whitcomb-bred Ebony series, pairing near-black foliage with crisp white flowers for high contrast.

directions: Ebony Glow pairs the Ebony series' signature near-black foliage with crisp white flower clusters, a high-contrast combination that reads more dramatically than white-flowered, green-leaved cultivars like Natchez. It grows as a dense, well-branched shrub or small tree to about 10 to 12 feet, holding its dark purple-black leaf color through summer heat before finishing the season in deep burgundy fall tones. It carries good resistance to powdery mildew relative to older all-indica cultivars, though full sun and open air circulation remain important for disease control. Deadhead spent panicles to prolong bloom, and avoid topping the plant; remove only dead or crossing branches in late winter.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Crape Myrtle Cultivars

common_name: Sarah's Favorite Crape Myrtle (Tall White-Flowered Heirloom Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Sarah's Favorite is an older, widely planted white-flowered Lagerstroemia indica cultivar that grows into a large tree with age.

directions: Sarah's Favorite is an older, widely planted Lagerstroemia indica cultivar producing abundant pure white flower clusters over a long summer bloom season on a fast-growing tree that can eventually reach 20 to 30 feet. Its smooth gray bark exfoliates only modestly compared to the National Arboretum's indica x fauriei hybrids, and as a straight indica selection it is somewhat more susceptible to powdery mildew than resistant cultivars like Natchez, so full sun and good air circulation help keep foliage clean. It has long been a staple of Southern nurseries and older landscapes for its dependable, heavy bloom and large mature size, making it well suited to a shade tree or specimen role. Prune only to remove dead, crossing, or sucker growth in late winter; never top the tree, which sacrifices its natural vase-shaped canopy.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Crape Myrtle Cultivars

common_name: Tightwad Red Crape Myrtle (Compact Reblooming Red Dwarf Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Tightwad Red is a genuinely dwarf, densely branched red-flowered crape myrtle from the same Louisiana breeding program that produced Dynamite.

directions: Tightwad Red is a dwarf, densely branched crape myrtle bred from the same Louisiana breeding program that produced Dynamite ('Whit II'), selected for a genuinely compact habit that stays under 5 feet without shearing. It produces bright true-red flower clusters over a long summer season and reblooms readily if spent panicles are removed. Its small size and tidy, rounded form make it well suited to foundation plantings, mixed borders, or mass plantings where full-size crape myrtle trees would quickly overwhelm the space. Give it full sun and good air circulation to minimize powdery mildew, and prune lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing twigs rather than shearing it into a hedge shape.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Crape Myrtle Cultivars
